'''Ted Doan''' was a businessman, philanthropist and the last member of the Dow family that served as president and CEO of the [[Dow Chemical Company]]. Doan led the company from 1962-71 and transformed Dow from a firm that made chemicals for other companies into one of the most widely known and one of the world’s largest chemical conglomerates. Doan was a strong supporter of entrepreneurship and was chairman of the [[Herbert H. and Grace A. Dow Foundation]], founded in his grandparents' honor.<ref name="DELTA">{{cite web |title=Herbert "Ted" Doan Scholarship Endowment |url=https://delta.academicworks.com/donors/herbert-ted-doan-scholarship-endowment |website=academicworks.com |publisher=Blackbaud, Inc |access-date=8 May 2025}}</ref>

==Early years==
Doan was born in 1922 in [[Midland, Michigan]]. He was the youngest of three children of [[Leland Doan|Leland Ira Doan]], general sales manager at Dow, and his wife, Ruth Alden Dow, daughter of the founder of Dow, [[Herbert H. Dow]], after whom he was named. He was always called '''Ted''' because his grandfather's name was "too much to hang on a kid" Doan recalled.<ref name=PASS/>
Doan attended elementary school in Midland before boarding at [[Cranbrook Educational Community|Cranbrook Academy]], then enrolled at [[Cornell University]]. Following the December [[Attack on Pearl Harbor]], Doan enlisted in the [[United States Army Air Corps]] and served as a meteorologist in [[World War II]]. When the conflict ended, he returned to Cornell and graduated in 1949 with a [[chemical engineering]] degree.<ref name="LEAD">{{cite web |last1=Marchlewski |first1=Kathie |title=Leader & friend |url=https://www.ourmidland.com/news/article/Leader-friend-7012239.php |website=ourmidland.com |publisher=Midland Daily News |access-date=8 May 2025}}</ref>

==Business==
Doan returned to Midland and was hired at Dow just weeks before [[Willard Dow]], his uncle, died in an airplane crash. Ted's father, Leland Doan, was named Dow president.<ref name=LEAD/> Ted Doan rapidly climbed the company ladder and followed his father, becoming president just thirteen years later when he was 40 years old.<ref name=BOOM/> 

Doan immediately integrated disparate company branches to create an efficient organization focused on growth and expansion outside the U.S.
His goal was to increase company earnings 10% each year.<ref name=PASS/> Dow sales surpassed $1 billion in 1964.<ref name="BOOM">{{cite web |title=The Post-War Boom |url=https://corporate.dow.com/en-us/about-dow/company/history/the-postwar-boom.html |website=corporate.dow.com |publisher=Dow |access-date=9 May 2025}}</ref>

Doan began an open-door policy for employees, placed higher emphasis on research, and held the attitude that their employees were the company's strength. Those policies continued after Doan's departure from Dow.<ref name=LEAD/>
Doan periodically visited the research labs at Dow and was always interested in the work of each employee.<ref name=LEAD/>

===Trioka===
Trioka is Russian term for a wagon pulled by a team of three horses abreast. Doan formed a management trioka at Dow with board chairman [[Carl Gerstacker]] responsible for finance and marketing; executive vice-president Ben Branch in charge of international business and manufacturing; Doan managed everything else. They met every other week on Monday mornings. Once each year they would retreat for a week to determine company strategy for the next year and evaluate all 300 senior managers. Upon their return, promotions and personnel changes were effected.<ref name=PASS/>

===Overseas===
When Dow realized that constructing manufacturing facilities in other countries created demand, they began producing plastics in Germany, Greece, Spain and Italy. The largest investment was in the [[Netherlands]], at [[Terneuzen]]. That chemical complex opened in 1965. Plants were also built in South America: Argentina and Colombia plus [[New Zealand]].<ref name=BOOM/>
With extensive operations all around the world, Doan and his managers had a meeting in 1965 where they acknowledged the need to decentralize. They established a headquarters on every continent to manage business. Dow Europe, Dow Latin America and Dow Pacific were established in 1966.
Technology centers were also established for 33 key products.<ref name=BOOM/>

==Retirement==
Doan stepped down from Dow in 1971 when global sales had achieved $2 billion<ref name=BOOM/> and Doan proclaimed that he and Dow were "healthy as horses".<ref name=PASS/> 
He believed that competent younger employees should be placed in senior positions because they have the new ideas and energy to advance the company. It really wasn't "retirement" for him; he was only 48. He remained on Dow's Board of Directors until 1987 and served on [[Dow Corning Corporation]]'s board until 1987<ref name="MTU">{{cite web |title=Herbert Doan |url=https://www.mtu.edu/chemical/department/alumni/profiles/herbert-doan.html |website=mtu.edu |publisher=Michigan Technological University |access-date=9 May 2025}}</ref> when he reached Dow's mandatory retirement age of 65. 

He founded venture capital firm ''Doan Associates'' in 1971,<ref name=MTU/> and in 1974, ''Doan Resources Corp.'', a small-business investment company.<ref name="PASS">{{cite web |title=Former Dow CEO Passes |url=https://www.agrimarketing.com/show_story.php?id=40632 |website=agrimarketing.com | publisher=Henderson Communications LLC. |access-date=9 May 2025}}</ref> 
He was co-founder and board member of biotechnology company [[Neogen]]<ref name=MTU/><ref>{{cite web |title=James and Judith Herbert: Survival and gratitude |url=https://www.lansingcitypulse.com/stories/james-and-judith-herbert-survival-and-gratitude,2007 |website=lansingcitypulse.com |publisher=City Pulse |date=9 May 2025}}</ref>

Doan continued working on projects until he became ill a few months before he passed.<ref name=LEAD/>

==Personal==
Doan married Donalda "Donnie" Lockwood in 1946.<ref name="ARTS">{{cite web |title=Doan, Herbert Dow |url=https://mcfta.pastperfectonline.com/byperson?keyword=Doan%2C%20Herbert%20Dow |website=pastperfectonline.com |publisher=Midland Center for the Arts |access-date=9 May 2025}}</ref> The couple had four children: Jeffrey (1947), Christine (1949), Michael (1953) and Ruth (1954).<ref name=DELTA/> When he took breaks from work, he went to the golf course for fun. He usually won, then enjoyed a coke and hotdog at the clubhouse.<ref name=LEAD/> After he left Dow, Doan married Anna Junia Cassell in 1975<ref name=ARTS/> and the union bore one child: Alexandria (1978).<ref name=DELTA/>
After battling abdominal issues for several months, Doan died May 16, 2006 at [[University of Michigan Medicine|UM Medical Center]] in Ann Arbor, Michigan. He was 83.<ref name=LEAD/>

==Accolades==
Former Dow CEO and chairman [[Andrew Liveris]] said, Ted Doan "was a man who understood that the gifts of wealth, position and intellect carried with them responsibilities to others."<ref name=LEAD/>
Doan did not self-promote. Another said former Dow CEO and chairman Bill Stavropoulos stated:
<blockquote>
"Ted Doan was probably the most open, generous and unpretentious person I have ever known. Almost every positive thing that has happened in Midland over the past 40 years had his imprint on it, but you would never know it. So much of what he did was low-key and often anonymous."<ref name=LEAD/> Doan initially refused to allow the Midland County Historical Society's building to bear his name "when in fact his name and Junia's should be on nearly every civic improvement project in this town...not to mention the many other good works they did in the state, in the country and across the world."<ref name=LEAD/>
</blockquote>

Regarding Doan's talent for giving advice, [[Northwood University]] President David Fry commented:
<blockquote>
"Some people are talkers and some people are listeners. Ted was a listener, then a thinker, then an integrator. He would ask [[Socratic questioning|Socratic questions]] in order for you to increase your own understanding of the context of your thoughts and where they were leading you."<ref name=LEAD/>
</blockquote>

[[Lawrence Reed]], president of the [[Mackinac Center for Public Policy]] lamented the passing of Doan:
<blockquote>
""Ted Doan was one of those people you meet only a few times in your life who impress you as a one-of-a-kind [[Polymath#Renaissance man|Renaissance citizen]]. He could connect with a Nobel laureate as readily as the guy next door. He was always kind, generous, thoughtful, smart and genuinely fun to be around. Ted will always be thought of not only as epitomizing Midland’s best, but as a gentleman of boundless character and an ambassador of goodwill to the country and beyond. He never borrowed from integrity to pay for expediency — a trait far too rare in the world these days."
<ref name="ONE">{{cite web |title=Mackinac Center President Comments on Passing of Herbert D. Doan, Chairman of the Dow Foundation |url=https://www.mackinac.org/7707 |website=mackinac.org |publisher=Mackinac Center for Public Policy |access-date=9 May 2025}}</ref>
</blockquote>

==Community involvement==
Doan was an early supporter of [[Saginaw Valley State University]]<ref name=LEAD/> and the Midland Law Enforcement Center.<ref name=LEAD/>
He was instrumental in establishing the Midland Community Foundation and construction of the [[The Tridge (Midland, Michigan)|Tridge]],<ref>{{cite web |title=Esther Gerstacker obituary |url=https://obits.mlive.com/us/obituaries/baycity/name/esther-gerstacker-obituary?id=14996025 |website=mlive.com |publisher=Legacy.com |access-date=7 May 2025}}</ref> a popular Midland landmark.
